per_run.approach_summary: Profiled all 200 continuous features for missingness, cardinality, marginal AUC, and target association; the signal was diffuse across many weak features, with no missing or low-cardinality columns. Compared regularized logistic regression, shrinkage LDA, ExtraTrees, LightGBM, and CatBoost using the same seeded 5-fold stratified splits. Shrinkage LDA gave the best standalone out-of-fold log loss (0.2412) and strong AUC (0.8564), consistent with a predominantly additive correlated-feature structure. Tree boosting added complementary nonlinear ranking signal: a 75% shrinkage-LDA / 12.5% LightGBM / 12.5% CatBoost probability blend improved out-of-fold log loss to 0.2371 and AUC to 0.8629. Final LDA was refit on all research rows; boosting predictions are averages across the five validation-trained models.

Profiled all 200 numeric features, missingness, duplicates, univariate associations, and row-order stability. Compared regularized logistic regression, random forests, extremely randomized trees, histogram boosting, and LightGBM with five-fold stratified out-of-fold predictions. The signal was diffuse and mainly additive: a standardized L2 logistic model (C=0.01, selected across a regularization grid) was strongest, while histogram boosting supplied complementary nonlinear signal. Final probabilities blend those models using an out-of-fold log-loss-optimized weight (0.792 logistic, 0.208 boosting), then refit both on all 5,000 rows.

I profiled all 200 numeric features, label prevalence, feature cardinality, univariate association, temporal label stability, and research-to-transfer mean shifts. I compared standardized ridge logistic regression, extremely randomized trees, LightGBM, tree ensembles, and restricted top-feature boosted models with five-fold stratified cross-validation. The signal was broad and approximately additive: ridge logistic regression produced the best validation log loss (about 0.245 at C=0.01) and strong AUC (about 0.846), while tree models or feature restriction did not improve it. A chronological last-1000-row holdout also favored this regularization and showed stable calibration; transfer marginal shifts were small. I therefore fit a standardized L2-logistic model with C=0.01 on all 5,000 research rows.

Profiled all 200 continuous anonymized features for cardinality, missingness, univariate association, mutual information, and train/transfer distribution stability. Compared stratified five-fold out-of-fold ridge logistic regression, shrinkage LDA, LightGBM across several tree capacities, ExtraTrees, and mutual-information feature subsets. Signal was broad and predominantly linear: shrinkage LDA achieved about 0.855 ROC AUC (about 0.241 log loss), versus about 0.842 for the best boosted-tree variant, and aggressive feature selection degraded performance. The final model uses all features and blends 75% automatically shrinkage-regularized LDA with 25% strongly regularized ridge logistic regression; this retained the ranking gain and improved out-of-fold probability calibration (about 0.238 log loss). Both components were refit on all 5000 rows.

Broad profiling found 200 dense numeric features, no missing or duplicate rows, many weak marginal signals (best single-feature AUC 0.593), and negligible research/transfer covariate shift (maximum single-feature domain AUC 0.524). I compared standardized regularized logistic regression, ExtraTrees, and LightGBM under stratified five-fold out-of-fold validation. Logistic regression was strongest on probability quality (AUC about 0.834, log loss about 0.259), consistent with a distributed approximately linear signal; trees were inferior, so the final predictor averages three nearby L2-regularized logistic fits around the CV-selected penalty. I attacked this result by changing fold seeds, checking row_id and target rates across row-id blocks, testing research-vs-transfer discrimination, and removing the 1, 3, and 10 strongest marginal features. The score remained broadly stable and no row-order or shift evidence suggested leakage; feature removal degraded performance rather than exposing dependence on one suspicious column. Thus I retained the regularized distributed model and used nearby-penalty averaging to reduce coefficient variance.

Profiled all 200 continuous features, marginal target associations and mutual information, correlations, missingness, duplicates, row-order behavior, and research/transfer shift. Compared regularized logistic regression, shrinkage LDA, quadratic discriminant analysis, random forests, extremely randomized trees, histogram boosting, and LightGBM under five-fold out-of-fold evaluation. Signal was diffuse and predominantly linear/covariance-aware: shrinkage LDA gave OOF AUC 0.8508/log loss 0.2453; C=0.01 logistic gave AUC 0.8443/log loss 0.2462. A convex blend selected solely on OOF log loss (60% shrinkage LDA, 40% logistic) improved log loss to 0.2431 while retaining AUC 0.8494. Nonlinear challengers were worse (best boosting AUC about 0.831). I attacked the linear blend as potentially exploiting shuffled-fold or cohort artifacts: repeated validation with contiguous row blocks left logistic AUC essentially unchanged (0.8376 versus 0.8381 in the matched run), prevalence across row-id chunks showed no directional pattern, and a flexible adversarial classifier could not distinguish research from transfer rows (AUC 0.494). I also checked that no single feature dominated and challenged with nonlinear models. The attack found no convincing leakage or distribution-shift evidence, so the final prediction is the full-data-fitted shrinkage-LDA/logistic blend.

I profiled all 200 continuous features, missingness, cardinality, duplicates, univariate signal, and research-to-transfer distribution shift, then compared regularized logistic regression, ExtraTrees, LightGBM, and their blends under five-fold stratified CV. The target was imbalanced (10.16% positive) and exhibited broad weak additive signal: ridge logistic gave the best calibrated performance (CV log loss about 0.245 at C=0.01; AUC about 0.845), while LightGBM reached similar AUC but materially worse log loss (about 0.277) and ExtraTrees was weaker. Sparse elastic-net variants did not improve log loss. I attacked the ridge result as possible fold, row-order, leakage, or shift exploitation: there were no exact duplicate feature rows, individual research-vs-transfer feature AUCs were all near chance (largest about 0.524), contiguous five-block CV remained essentially unchanged (AUC about 0.844, log loss about 0.245), and held-out later blocks remained predictive. Coefficients learned on disjoint halves were directionally consistent, though noisier as expected from the smaller samples. This did expose the boosted model's overconfidence rather than evidence against the linear model, so I selected a strongly regularized all-feature ridge logistic fit on all 5,000 rows, with no row_id feature and no tree blend.

Explored all 200 features using missingness, cardinality, duplication, marginal AUC, feature correlation, and research/transfer distribution checks. The features were nearly uncorrelated and individually weak, while signal was distributed broadly. Five-fold CV compared regularized logistic regression, selected-feature linear models, LDA, ExtraTrees, LightGBM, CatBoost, Gaussian naive Bayes, quantile transforms, and smoothed quantile-bin likelihood models. Gaussian NB captured stable class-specific marginal shifts best (about 0.876 AUC); flexible binned densities and tree ensembles alone were worse. I attacked this result as possible fold/leakage or sequential-row artifact: five different shuffled fold seeds gave AUC 0.874-0.877, contiguous unshuffled folds gave 0.875, no duplicates or missing values existed, and smoothing/flexible-density sweeps did not reveal a brittle gain. Half-sample models were less identical, as expected with only about 250 positives each, so I reduced variance using five fold models. The final prediction averages fold-model log odds and uses a conservative OOF-chosen 75% Gaussian-NB / 25% LightGBM blend with fixed logistic calibration; this slightly improved OOF AUC (0.8774) and log loss (0.2227) over calibrated NB.

DATA. 5,000 labelled rows, 1,500 unlabelled, 200 anonymised continuous features, base rate
10.16%. No missing values, no research/transfer distribution shift (max standardised mean
shift 0.08 sd). All 200 features are essentially mutually independent (max |pairwise
correlation| 0.051 over 6,500 rows, exactly the null level; flat PCA spectrum) -- so no
latent factor structure to exploit.

WHAT I FOUND (the structure, not just a score).
1. Signal is DENSE, not sparse. Univariate AUCs top out at 0.594/0.407, but a ridge logistic
   on all 200 features reaches CV AUC 0.849. Unregularised Wald |z| scores across the 200
   coefficients match z ~ N(0, 2.3) almost exactly (82 with |z|>2, 37 with |z|>3, vs 77/39
   predicted) -- i.e. effectively EVERY feature carries a small effect. Capacity-matched
   GBMs top out around 0.83-0.85: trees are the wrong hypothesis class for a dense additive
   signal in 200 dimensions.
2. Every per-feature effect is CONVEX, and curvature is always positive. Score tests for
   z_j^2 against the linear fit gave 43 features at |z|>2, all positive, and |curvature|
   correlates 0.50 with |linear coefficient|. Fitted per-feature shape functions are convex
   in every case (monotone but with the action concentrated in one tail).
3. That convexity is a CLASS-CONDITIONAL VARIANCE effect. Var(x_j | y=1) / Var(x_j | y=0)
   has mean 1.07, is >1 for essentially every feature (29 at z>2, none at z<-2). Fitting
   log(v1/v0) against the squared mean shift gives log(v1/v0) ~= 0.046 + 1.30*(m1-m0)^2:
   a uniform global dispersion term plus a feature-specific term tied to that feature's own
   mean shift. Consequence: positives are partly a *dispersion* class, so sum_j z_j^2 alone
   gives AUC 0.729, and it keeps working on the 100 weakest features (AUC 0.61) -- the
   dispersion effect is spread over all 200 features, not concentrated in the strong ones.
4. The FEATURES themselves are latent-bit encoded. Pooled excess kurtosis is -0.50 (strongly
   platykurtic); per-feature 2-component Gaussian mixtures fit far better than a normal and
   recover, for every feature, a ~50/50 mixture with means near -0.73/+0.73 sd and component
   sd ~0.68 -- one hidden binary per feature carrying about half its variance. But the label
   is NOT a function of those bits: a model on posterior bit log-odds reaches only 0.856 vs
   0.872 for the same model on the raw values, so the continuous within-component position
   matters and the bit decode is a distributional fact, not the mechanism.
5. The model is genuinely ADDITIVE. Screening all 990 pairwise products among the 45
   strongest features against the additive-model residual gave a perfectly null z
   distribution (sd 1.00, max |z| 3.25, one |z|>3 where 2.7 are expected). No interactions.
6. All 200 features SHARE THE SAME SHAPE. This was the biggest single win. Log-density-ratio
   per feature is well described by g1(z)*a_j + g2(z)*b_j with g1, g2 common to all features
   and only the two loadings feature-specific. The learned g1 is monotone but flat in the
   middle and steep in the tails, then saturating past |z|~2.4; g2 is U-shaped but flattens
   at the extreme left -- both clearly non-quadratic, which is why a Gaussian model leaves
   signal on the table. Allowing per-feature deviations from the shared shape (hierarchical
   GAM, penalty swept over a decade) only ever *hurt*, confirming the shapes are genuinely
   common.

MODELLING PATH (all figures = repeated stratified 5-fold CV, 3-5 seeds).
  ridge logistic, all 200 features ............ AUC 0.849
  + per-feature squares ....................... AUC 0.863
  penalised additive spline GAM ............... AUC 0.872
  Gaussian naive Bayes ........................ AUC 0.872 / logloss 0.231
  structured NB: empirical-Bayes shrunk mean
    shifts + log-variance ratios replaced by
    the fitted 0.046 + 1.30*dm^2 law .......... AUC 0.877 / logloss 0.225
  shared-shape model (final base) ............. AUC 0.883 / logloss 0.219
The structured-NB step matters because the raw per-feature log-variance ratio has an
empirical-Bayes shrinkage factor of only 0.22 (it is almost pure noise at 508 positives);
predicting it from the mean shift instead removes nearly all that noise.

FINAL MODEL. Shared-shape model as described: NB-derived loadings (a_j from the shrunk mean
shift, b_j from the structured variance term), a 6-knot cubic B-spline basis, and the two
aggregate designs sum_j a_j*B(z_ij) and sum_j b_j*B(z_ij) fed to a ridge logistic. Blended in
score space with a penalised spline GAM (weight 0.10) and a LightGBM (weight 0.15) -- both
small weights, both improving every seed, chosen on a flat region of the weight surface.
CV-bagged over 5 seeds x 5 folds; transfer scores averaged over the 25 fold models and mapped
to probabilities by a quadratic-logit calibrator fitted on the out-of-fold scores. Features
standardised using research + transfer rows (unsupervised use only).

Honest out-of-fold estimate for this exact ensemble: AUC 0.889, logloss 0.2135, mean predicted
probability 0.1016 against a 0.1016 base rate. Predicted transfer mean is 0.1053.

WHAT DID NOT WORK, and why it is informative: quantile/Gaussian-rank alignment of features
(0.882 -> hurts; the shared shape lives on the natural scale), per-feature Gaussian-mixture
naive Bayes (0.852; too many parameters for 508 positives), discriminative or moment-based
alternating refit of the loadings (0.877/0.883 -> no gain; the closed-form moment estimates are
already at the noise floor), extra global dispersion moments beyond the shared shape (no gain;
already absorbed), and boosting LightGBM from the NB score as an offset (0.875).

PROBLEM STRUCTURE FOUND. 200 anonymized features, 5000 labeled rows (10.16% positive), 1500 transfer rows.

EDA. Features are mutually independent: the 200x200 correlation eigenspectrum of the pooled 6500 rows matches Marchenko-Pastur for p/n=0.031 almost exactly (support [0.68,1.38] observed vs [0.68,1.38] predicted), max |r| = 0.051 across 19,900 pairs, zero pairs above 0.06. Marginals are symmetric (mean |skew| 0.086), bounded at about +/-2.95 sd, with mean excess kurtosis -0.50 (sub-Gaussian, uniform-sum-like). No research/transfer shift: adversarial-validation LR AUC 0.507, 4/200 KS tests at p<0.01, feature means/variances match within noise. row_id shows no drift in base rate or features.

WHAT DRIVES THE LABEL. Two components, both dense.
(1) A dense linear direction: 90/200 features have univariate |AUC-0.5| > 2 SE (9 expected by chance); L1 is far worse than L2 (0.81 vs 0.85), so the signal is dense, not sparse. Ridge logistic on the 200 standardized features gives OOF AUC 0.851.
(2) An ISOTROPIC QUADRATIC / 'extremeness' component that a linear model cannot see. Score-testing all 200 x_j^2 terms against the linear model's residual gave 161/200 positive with mean z = +1.31 -- a systematic, same-sign convexity in every feature. Pooling residuals across all 200 features by |z| bin traces a clean symmetric U: rows that are extreme in ANY feature are more likely positive. sum(z_j^2) alone scores AUC 0.729; the best single isotropic statistic is sum|z_j|^3 at 0.737. Crucially, ONE shared isotropic term beats 200 free per-feature quadratic coefficients (0.877 vs 0.865), i.e. the effect is genuinely rotationally symmetric, not 200 separate curvatures.

MECHANISM. Class-conditional statistics confirm an exponential-tilt / diagonal-QDA generator: class 1 has a dense mean shift (per-feature sd 0.125 vs 0.047 expected under the null, permutation z=35) AND a uniform ~3.4% per-feature sd inflation (mean log variance ratio +0.064, permutation z=15.6). Neither class shows any off-diagonal covariance structure (class-1 off-diagonal r sd 0.0442 vs 0.0444 expected from n=508). So class 1 is class 0 tilted by exp(sum_j w_j z_j + sum_j a_j z_j^2) with a_j > 0. Equivalently the decision surface is an ELLIPSOID: positives lie outside an ellipsoid centred at c = -w/(2a). This also predicts, and I confirmed, corr(|mean shift_j|, variance inflation_j) = 0.33-0.40, the second-order coupling the tilt implies. A permutation test after regressing out that d^2 coupling still shows real per-feature heterogeneity in a_j (z=4.64, EB shrinkage factor 0.43), so a lightly-shrunk per-feature quadratic block earns a further ~+0.004.

NEGATIVE RESULTS THAT MATTER. All 19,900 pairwise interaction score tests are null (sd of z = 1.055, max |z| = 3.96, zero above 4 where 1.25 are expected) -- there are NO pairwise interactions. LightGBM tuned over leaves/rounds tops out at 0.839-0.841, well below the linear model, because trees cannot represent a dense 200-term isotropic quadratic. A flexible shared even-function basis (8 |z|-bin count features) does not beat the single sum|z|^3 term (0.8823 vs 0.8823), confirming the shared shape is essentially quadratic-to-cubic and fully captured.

FINAL MODEL. Ridge logistic on three blocks with separate penalties: 200 linear terms (lambda 5000), 200 standardized z_j^2 terms (lambda 15000, heavy shrinkage toward the shared value), and one sum|z_j|^3 term (lambda 6000). Blended 0.8/0.2 with an independent empirical-Bayes diagonal-QDA estimator whose shrinkages (kw=0.852 for the mean shift, ka=0.43 for the log-variance ratios) are derived analytically from the data rather than tuned. Bagged over 10 seeds x 5 folds; probabilities Platt-scaled on the out-of-fold scores. Per-seed OOF AUC 0.8828 +/- 0.0013; bagged-OOF AUC 0.8857; OOF log-loss 0.216 vs 0.329 for the base rate; OOF calibration deciles track actual rates within 0.008 everywhere.

SELF-ATTACK. I tried to break the claim that the +0.031 AUC from the isotropic term is real rather than a research-row artifact.
(a) Standardization leakage: I fit the scaler on research+transfer combined, which could in principle let the norm feature carry information. Refitting the scaler inside each training fold only, with fresh CV seeds, gives 0.8814 -- unchanged.
(b) Hyperparameter overfitting: the three block penalties were picked from a 125-point grid on the same CV. Fully nested CV, re-selecting penalties inside every training fold, gives 0.8819 -- unchanged. The untuned EB-QDA estimator independently reaches 0.8789, so the result does not depend on the grid.
(c) Outlier-driven: winsorizing every feature at +/-2.5 sd leaves the model at 0.8848 (identical) and the linear-only baseline at 0.8530; even at +/-2.0 sd the quadratic gain is intact (0.8807 vs 0.8484). Dropping each row's 10 most extreme features still leaves the norm statistic at AUC 0.686. So it is not a handful of extreme rows.
(d) Subset replication: a random half of 100 features gives norm AUC 0.661, the other half 0.682 -- the effect is spread over all 200 features, which a spurious feature could not produce. Splitting research by row_id into two contiguous blocks of 2500 and training on one, testing on the other, reproduces the gain both ways (0.8741 vs 0.8355; 0.8804 vs 0.8477).
(e) Is CV itself optimistic? I built a parametric simulator from the fitted tilt (bootstrapped real feature marginals, model-generated labels) and ran the identical pipeline on 6 replicates: mean CV AUC 0.8744 vs mean held-out transfer AUC 0.8750 -- CV is unbiased here. The same simulation puts the Bayes ceiling at 0.8935, i.e. about 0.012-0.019 of the gap to Bayes is irreducible estimation noise from having only 508 positives to fit a 200-dimensional direction; ridge, EB-QDA, and diagonal-QDA all land within 0.001 of each other at that frontier, so there is little left to win.
The attack failed on every front, so I finalized this approach. The one caveat I cannot test locally: transfer AUC on 1500 rows (~150 positives) has a sampling SE of roughly 0.017, so the realized score will scatter around 0.88 regardless of the model.
